sceneHappening: The empty tomb, the road to Emmaus, and the risen Jesus with his disciples
summary: On the first day of the week, at early dawn, the women come to the tomb with the spices they have prepared and find the stone rolled away and the body gone. While they are perplexed, two men in dazzling clothes stand by them and say, "Why do you seek the living among the dead? He isn't here, but is risen. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee, saying that the Son of Man must be delivered up into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again." They remember his words, return from the tomb, and tell all this to the eleven and the rest. The women are Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them. "These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn't believe them." But Peter gets up and runs to the tomb, stoops and sees the linen cloths by themselves, and goes home wondering. That same day two of them are going to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, talking about all that had happened. Jesus himself draws near and walks with them, but their eyes are kept from recognizing him. "What are you talking about?" One of them, named Cleopas, says, "Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn't know the things which have happened there in these days?" They tell him about Jesus of Nazareth, "a prophet mighty in deed and word," whom the chief priests and rulers delivered up to be condemned and crucified: "But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel." It is the third day, and some women of their company astonished them, saying they had not found the body and had seen a vision of angels, who said he was alive. "Some of us went to the tomb, and found it just like the women had said, but they didn't see him." He says, "Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Didn't the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?" Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explains to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. As they draw near the village he acts as if he would go further, but they urge him, "Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over." At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them, and their eyes are opened, and they recognize him, and he vanishes from their sight. They say to one another, "Weren't our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?" They rise that very hour and return to Jerusalem, where they find the eleven and those with them saying, "The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!" They tell what happened on the road and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. As they speak, Jesus himself stands among them: "Peace be to you." They are terrified, thinking they see a spirit. "Why are you troubled? ... See my hands and my feet, that it is truly me. Touch me and see, for a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." While they still disbelieve for joy and wonder, he asks, "Do you have anything here to eat?" They give him a piece of broiled fish, and he takes it and eats in front of them. He says, "These are my words which I spoke to you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled." Then he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures: "Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things. Behold, I send out the promise of my Father on you. But wait in the city of Jerusalem, until you are clothed with power from on high." He leads them out as far as Bethany, lifts up his hands, and blesses them, and while he blesses them he is parted from them and carried up into heaven. They worship him and return to Jerusalem with great joy, and are continually in the temple, blessing God.
whySettingMatters: Luke's resurrection chapter is built around Scripture and a meal. The Emmaus story has two disciples, one named Cleopas, walking away from Jerusalem, and the risen Jesus joins them and does what the whole Gospel has been doing: opens the Scriptures and breaks bread. Emmaus was about seven miles (sixty stadia) from Jerusalem, but where it was is debated, since several sites have been proposed. Their statement, "We were hoping he would redeem Israel," gives voice to what many expected, a national rescue. Jesus' reply about the Christ's necessary suffering and glory points back to the passages like Isaiah 53 and the Psalms, and he names the three parts of the Hebrew Scriptures: the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms (24:44). That the women are first to tell, and are not believed, would have been striking in a world where women's testimony was given less weight; Luke notes it without softening. Jesus' eating the fish answers the disciples' fear that he is a ghost. "The promise of my Father" is the Holy Spirit, who comes in Acts 2, and "beginning from Jerusalem" to "all nations" sets up the structure of Acts. Luke's ending, with joy and blessing in the temple, returns to where the Gospel began: the temple, a priest, and praise.

questions: The women are not believed. How does Luke want us to hear that, and how did they hear it?
"Weren't our hearts burning within us?" What was it about how Jesus explained the Scriptures?
They recognize him in the breaking of bread. Why that moment?
Jesus tells them to wait until they are clothed with power. What does Luke seem to say that the disciples need next?
